subject: Chemistry
title: Maple Syrup: Tree Blood to Sweetness
description: One-minute skill: Maple Syrup: Tree Blood to Sweetness.

hook.text: Maple syrup starts as 2% sugar sap. Boiling 40 liters of sap down to 1 liter concentrates it to 66% sugar.

buildup.text: In spring, maple trees pump sap upward using freeze-thaw pressure cycles. Tapping a hole captures the flow.

discovery.text: The sap is mostly sucrose dissolved in water. Boiling evaporates water and triggers Maillard reactions for flavor.

twist.text: Maple syrup contains over 300 flavor compounds not found in the original sap—all created during boiling.

climax.text: Quebec produces 70% of the world's maple syrup. They have a strategic maple syrup reserve—like oil reserves.

punchline.text: 40 liters of sap, one liter of syrup. Boiling concentrates sugar and creates flavor.

quiz.question: How much sap is needed to make one liter of maple syrup?
options: About 40 liters—most of it is water that gets boiled off
About 5 liters—maple sap is already very sweet
About 100 liters—the process is extremely wasteful

details.summary: Maple syrup is produced by boiling down the sap of sugar maple trees, concentrating sucrose from about two percent to sixty-six percent..
details.whyItMatters: Maple syrup production is a unique intersection of tree biology and food chemistry. It supports a multi-billion dollar industry primarily in Quebec, which produces over seventy percent of the global supply.
takeaways: Forty liters of sap must be boiled down to produce one liter of syrup
The Maillard reaction during boiling creates over 300 flavor compounds
Sap flows when freeze-thaw cycles create pressure changes in the tree

faq.question: Why does maple sap flow only during the spring freeze-thaw season?
faq.answer: Freezing nights cause gases dissolved in sap to contract, drawing water into the tree through osmosis. During the day, warming temperatures expand the gases, creating positive pressure that pushes sap out through tap holes. This cycle stops when sustained warm temperatures arrive.

faq.question: Why does maple syrup grade and color vary from early to late season?
faq.answer: Early-season sap produces lighter, more delicately flavored syrup because it contains fewer amino acids and microorganisms. As the season progresses, bacterial activity in tap holes increases amino acid content, producing more Maillard reaction products, darker color, and stronger flavor.
